Breaking.title: Jeffrey Donaldson to be interviewed over alleged rape inside Houses of Parliament
Breaking.text:
Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.

The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.

Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.

It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.

The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.

While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.

It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.

"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.

She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.

On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.

But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.

Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London was raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year.

A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.

Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

Breaking.title: Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
Breaking.text:
Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.

Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and its European allies have been pressing Moscow for an immediate resumption of the talks suspended in February, and Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, possibly in Abu Dhabi.

Russia has for months refused talks as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.

Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland on Monday in Oslo. Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The talks, however, were put on hold, with the Kremlin blaming last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes on Russia during its general elections for their disruption.

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".

"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

The talks in Oslo and St Petersburg were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

European leaders have expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia.

Breaking.title: Aberfan disaster: Royal Family pay respects to 'most tragic of days imaginable'
Breaking.text:
The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary.

Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school.

The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit".

Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing

About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside.

Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris.

The coal waste had been piled high on the side of Mynydd Merthyr – above Aberfan – for years, even though there were numerous underground springs below.

An official inquiry in 1967 found the National Coal Board was responsible for the Aberfan disaster, but survivors and bereaved families have long pointed to a litany of injustices.

Money was taken from the public disaster fund to help pay for the removal of remaining coal tips above the village, while compensation payments were limited and survivors had to undergo repeated assessments.

Support to help deal with their trauma was also minimal.

Professor Iain McLean, the co-author of Aberfan - Government and Disaster, has questioned why nobody was ever prosecuted for the Aberfan disaster.

Speaking on the BBC Radio Wales Phone In on Wednesday, he said: "And so one of the other failures of the government of the day is their, to me, incomprehensible failure to sack Lord Robens and his senior directors."

Robens was the chairman of the National Coal Board at the time, and had faced numerous complaints about the dangers that loomed a quarter of a mile high above the village.

One of these included a petition from Pantglas school in 1963, three years before the disaster.

In 1997, McLean met three of the counsels who had appeared before the 1967 tribunal and asked why no legal action was taken.

"They all said 'nobody thought of it at the time'," he said.

On Wednesday the royal party met retired members of the emergency services at the community centre who helped in the hours and days after the disaster.

They then spent time with survivors, bereaved parents, and siblings of those who died.

In a speech to those in the community centre, King Charles said the disaster "was and always will be, the saddest and most tragic of days imaginable".

He said: "Over the years, as once again today, it has been profoundly humbling to hear the testimonies of survivors of relatives who lost their loved ones, and of rescuers who fought so hard to save others during this appalling tragedy."

"Today in our nation and across the world, thoughts will turn to you in Aberfan, hearts far from this valley will ache with yours."

Prince William also visited Ynysowen Community Primary School to unveil an Aberfan Memorial Tree.

The tree was designed and created by ArtMetal, a family-run metalwork company based in Rhayader, Powys.

The concept was developed by school headteacher Simone Roden, along with Edwards who is vice chair of governors at the school.

During the early planning stages, pupils helped shape the vision of the memorial by sharing drawings and ideas.

During the visit, Prince William met pupils and heard them recite poems they had written about the disaster and read memories recorded by the children who survived.

"Well done guys," William told the pupils.

"It shows the next generation does care about them, and it matters."

Before unveiling the sculpture, he watched the pupils perform the Aberfan Song and well-known children's song Everyone Belongs.

Breaking.title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
Breaking.text:
The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".

She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.

"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."

Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.

The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.

The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.

The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.

"We think about it a lot."

In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".

They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."

Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".

"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."

"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."

The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.

It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".

The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

Breaking.title: Masked boy guilty of trying to murder schoolgirl in Norfolk
Breaking.text:
A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.

The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.

Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.

The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.

Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.

The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.

The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

CCTV footage captured the moment the girl was stabbed in the back, before her attacker ran off while "pursued by a teacher".

The victim described to the jury how, in the aftermath of the attack, she had told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed".

In a police interview played to the court, the girl said she was in "panic mode" and felt numb and weak.

Chris Paxton KC, prosecuting, said it was "sheer good fortune" the "defenceless and vulnerable" pupil was not seriously hurt.

"This was a knife strike delivered, we the prosecution say, as an attempt to kill," he added.

He messaged his mother to say "I'm sorry" shortly after the attack, jurors heard.

"I was in complete shock," she told the court.

Breaking.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027 coach tickets oversold in admin error
Breaking.text:
An administrative error resulted in coach journeys to the Glastonbury Festival being oversold through its official ticketing partner.

More coach package tickets were sold for certain departures than there are seats available, according to an email See Tickets sent to customers.

Those affected will not lose their tickets however. Instead, their booking will automatically be converted into a general admission ticket and the coach fare will be refunded.

The ticketing agency declined to comment further, but the BBC understands Glastonbury Festival was not responsible for the error.

Glastonbury coach ticket prices range from £26 to £185 - on top of general admission - depending on the departure town or city and whether it is a single or return journey.

Affected customers have been told that unless they opt to keep their coach seat by 31 October 2026, their booking will automatically be converted to general admission.

The coach fare will then be refunded to the card used for the original booking.

See Tickets' customer services department assured customers the error will not affect festival deposits, and ticket holders will be able to pay the remaining balance for their tickets as normal in April.

The agency apologised and thanked customers for their understanding, adding: "We're looking forward to welcoming you to the festival in June."

Breaking.title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
Breaking.text:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth £40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

Alias came to our attention during a wider BBC probe into illegal working and criminality linked to some High Street businesses, including mini-marts and barbershops.

His name was mentioned in social media videos, including on Kurdish Facebook pages, where business owners in the UK praised his ability to resolve problems linked to immigration fines.

For months we monitored these videos, which carried Alias's name, that of his law firm, Liberty Solicitors, and a mobile phone number. Some had more than 20,000 views.

In one, a Kurdish-speaking shop owner explained that, after having been issued with a penalty for employing an illegal worker, he had "tried two or three different places to get it sorted but nobody could resolve it".

He went on to say that "Mr Alias" had got the fine cancelled - showing a letter as evidence.

Alias told the BBC he had not commissioned, paid for, approved or circulated videos on social media.

Watch the full film of Ed Thomas's investigation here, external

Our reporter contacted Alias on the phone, claiming to be a business owner who faced a fine after immigration officers had found somebody working at his mini-mart illegally.

There was no actual shop, worker, or fine.

During the call, which we recorded, Alias told our reporter his services would cost 10% of the fine - in this case, £4,500 - and he would want money up front.

Alias explained how liability for the fine could be shifted to somebody outside the UK, if that person could be named as owner of the business.

"Do you have anybody's name who we can use? Anybody who's gone back to Iraq, gone back to Iran?" he asked.

He then offered a fictitious example: "Say we put forward Karwan, yeah? Then fine come on Karwan's name. Karwan not here, Karwan in Iraq."

What Alias appeared to be proposing was the use of a "ghost director" - in other words, someone who is paid to put their name on official documents, thereby masking the real owner of a business.

Using ghost directors is a widespread illegal practice, the law enforcement official told us.

An employer in the UK, who hires a worker with no legal right to work, faces being fined.

In 2024, the maximum penalty for knowingly employing illegal workers rose from £15,000 to £60,000.

A total of 5,755 fines were issued for illegal working between 2021-2025, the Home Office has told us. These would have been worth a total of £215m, but only £60.5m has been collected.

The Home Office points out that not all fines issued in the past five years would have been paid during the same time period, and the amount collected would always be lower than the value of the fines, because of appeals or discounts for fast payment.

Fitted with a secret camera, our reporter went to Alias's office in Bradford with £250 as an upfront payment.

Alias seemed annoyed, having originally asked for £500, and made a show of counting out the notes, but did not provide a receipt.

Our reporter had by this time told Alias he had found someone in the Kurdish Region of Iraq ready to declare they were the owner of the mini-mart business.

From Alias's office, the reporter rang this supposed contact, a man who gave his name as Saman. In reality, Saman was another BBC undercover journalist based in the UK.

As a solicitor, Alias could only ethically argue the case for transferring the fine if Saman were to declare to him, either verbally or in writing, that he was the real owner of the business.

In our secret recording of their conversation, Alias repeatedly asks Saman to confirm this, despite knowing there is a question mark over the mini-mart's true ownership.

Alias's frustration appears to mount with each attempt.

Alias: "Am I right in thinking that you are the owner of the shop and I'm going to write to them explaining that you're the owner of the shop?"

Saman: "I'm not the owner of the shop, but I'm ready to transfer it to my name."

Alias: "OK, but I'm going to be writing to them [the authorities] to explain that you're the owner of the shop."

Saman: "I am happy to do that yeah but also you do know, I am not the owner of the shop? And I've not even seen this shop before!"

Alias: "If you're saying that to me, then I can't do that. You understand? I can only do it if you're telling me, you are the owner of the shop."

Alias then tries to reassure Saman, telling him: "They might say, 'OK, you have to pay this money.' We don't pay the money. That's the end of it. Case finished."

Asked if he has handled similar cases, Alias tells Saman he does it "all the time for people who get fines".

We showed our recordings to Bryony Rest, who described Alias's conduct as amounting to "perverting the course of justice", and said he should be struck off.

She also noticed from the recording that, late in his meeting with the two reporters, Alias's manner suddenly changed, as if he had become suspicious.

"I can't advance an untruthful or dishonest... version of events," he is heard saying, before telling the men to decide among themselves who owns the shop.

However, Rest noted that it had been Alias himself who originally suggested "the untruthful version of events".

Later, Alias sent the undercover reporter a series of messages appearing to withdraw his offer of help.

In a subsequent phone call, he repeated that he would not pursue an untruthful claim and said he would arrange for the £250 down payment to be repaid.

The money has still not been returned, but Alias says Liberty Solicitors has made numerous attempts to return the cash.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told us the new review into the illegal-working fines scheme would aim "to ensure we are able to respond to non-compliance and non-payment through all available means".

Alias has denied ever advising anyone to put a penalty into the name of someone who was not responsible for a business, or to give false information to the Home Office, and said he never would.

"My work is to challenge penalties lawfully, through the routes Parliament has provided, usually on the basis that the person found was not an employee at all," Alias told the BBC.

He added that when our reporter proposed putting his business into someone else's name, Alias had told him in writing he could not advance an untruthful or dishonest case and did not act for him.

Breaking.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
Breaking.text:
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.

He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.

The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere.

At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined.

Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment.

"And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court.

Breaking.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain
Breaking.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.

Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.

Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".

It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.

Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.

Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.

Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.

The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.

Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...

"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."

On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".

He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.

"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."

"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.

Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.

The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.

It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.

While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.

Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

Breaking.title: Helen Haines: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
Breaking.text:
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.

Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".

The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.

Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.

"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.

"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.

Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.

He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.

In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.

Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.

"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."

Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.

Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.

Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".

The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.

Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.

"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.

"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.

Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.

Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.

The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.

Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.

In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.

There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.

Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.

Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.

Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.

Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".

"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.

"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

Breaking.title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
Breaking.text:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

Breaking.title: The Gambia to pay Yahya Jammeh victims from the proceeds of the ex-president's seized US mansion
Breaking.text:
The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said.

The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation.

The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds".

Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.

On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.

It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".

Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.

He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.

Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.

In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.

A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.

There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.

Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.

A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

Business.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
Business.text:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.

She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".

"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.

The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.

She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.

"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.

The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".

He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".

Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.

"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.

He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."

Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.

But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

Business.title: Inflation and borrowing data illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
Business.text:
The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.

From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.

The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.

The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.

Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.

These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.

On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.

While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.

The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.

The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.

Business.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
Business.text:
UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.

The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts.

Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.

It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.

The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

Business.title: UK inflation: What is the rate and why are prices still rising?
Business.text:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.

Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.

The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.

The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), external, and the latest figure is published every month.

The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.

Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.

But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.

For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.

Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.

The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.

Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.

But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.

Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.

Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.

But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.

When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.

As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.

As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.

Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.

Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.

The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.

The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data, external - up from 3.2% in August.

The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.

US inflation was in 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.

The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.

The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

Business.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
Business.text:
The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues.

KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn.

There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget.

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Your First Home scheme

Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out.

The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.

There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

Business.title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
Business.text:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".

A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.

Business.title: Google says cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites resolved
Business.text:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase.

Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money.

"Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC.

"This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time."

She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions.

"It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added.

More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday.

A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage.

"We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout.

"We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services.

A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon".

Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hours during an outage at AWS' largest cloud site.

Experts say this latest outage show how many businesses still rely on core services provided by a few large cloud operators.

"Google Cloud's outage is a reminder of how deeply our economies depend on just a handful of cloud providers," said Prof Feng Li, associate dean for research & innovation at Bayes Business School.

He added that it was not yet clear what caused the power problem identified by Google Cloud.

"Large cloud systems are complex, and failures will happen.

"What matters is how far they spread, how quickly services recover and whether customers have workable alternatives," he added.

Business.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
Business.text:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.

The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

Business.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
Business.text:
The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City.

The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September.

No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case.

It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than £900m. City are appealing the verdict.

The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs.

The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules.

It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies.

BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm.

The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme.

Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases.

He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules.

"This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account.

"The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability."

BDO declined to comment.

Business.title: LIV Golf: Former Open champion Louis Oosthuizen quits league
Business.text:
Former Open Championship winner Louis Oosthuizen has become the latest high-profile player to quit LIV Golf, describing it as the "hardest decision he has had to make in his career".

The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its multibillion-dollar backing.

Oosthuizen, 44, joined LIV Golf in 2022 and was captain of the Southern Guards GC team.

The South African now plans to return to the DP World Tour in 2027.

"Five years ago, I made one of the best decisions of my life, moving away from the traditional golf world and into something very special with LIV Golf and Southern Guards GC," Oosthuizen posted on social media.

"I'm the biggest supporter of team golf and always will be. Golf needs more of it.

"This is probably the hardest decision I've had to make in my career, but I have to do what I believe is right for my golf."

The 2010 Open champion, who has finished as a runner-up at least once in each of the other three majors, said a more flexible playing schedule will help him to compete at a high level.

"I realised I have a lot more in me, and my biggest fear was that the schedule on LIV 2.0 would be tough to manage," said former world number four Oosthuizen.

"I feel I have a few more years of good, competitive golf left in me, and the only way to be really sharp and competitive is through a schedule I control."

Oosthuizen joins Thomas Pieters, Sergio Garcia, Abraham Ancer, David Puig and Adrian Meronk in announcing his departure.

Last week, two-time major winner Jon Rahm gave up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement.

Some former LIV Golf players, including Brooks Koepka, have since rejoined the PGA Tour, which rewrote its rules in December to allow the five-time major winner to return, subject to certain sanctions.

Guy Kinnings, CEO of the DP World Tour, told BBC Sport earlier this month that players who continue with LIV will not be allowed to be members of the European tour next season.

Business.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge share giveaways
Business.text:
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.

Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.

The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".

Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.

The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.

Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.

In a post on social media,, external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."

It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."

Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.

The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.

Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.

Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.

Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI, with that figure rising as high as ​60% in advanced economies.

In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.

Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year....
