articles.title: ‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build America
articles.text:
Every morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.

Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.

They’re on their way to work too. But the federal agents who form this second army are on a different mission.

Unlike the builders, they are not forging the US’s future one new starter home at a time. Their job is to pursue those who do the building: they follow the framers, track down the roofers, chase the cement masons and concrete finishers.

They are hunters.

“In Texas, you go deer hunting in the early morning,” said Jacob Monty, an immigration lawyer in Houston. “That’s what they are doing. They are hunting for construction workers, early in the morning, like you would an animal.”

Texas and its construction workforce are the ground zero of Donald Trump’s latest mass deportation effort, dubbed ICE 2.0. As the US president has pivoted from last year’s militarized “invasions” of Los Angeles and Minneapolis to this year’s less visible but no less devastating stop-and-search tactics, he has found rich pickings in Texas.

Texas is seeing by far the greatest number of ICE arrests in the country. More than 12,000 in July alone, almost double the number in the next most affected states, Florida and California.

Many of the detainees are Hispanic builders. Of every 10 construction workers in Texas, four are foreign born, most of whom are Hispanic and undocumented.

“This is low-hanging fruit,” Monty said. “If you target Texas Hispanics in trucks, you have a good chance of nabbing an undocumented person, and feeding the mass deportation machine.”

But there is a price to pay for ICE casting its dragnet through Texas barrios and building sites as it seeks to meet its new target of 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The street-level apprehensions are roiling the state, distorting its economy, forcing up house prices and the cost of groceries.

Hispanic families are also being torn apart. Hardworking people are being pushed into the shadows, others disappearing as they flee the country or are deported. The foundations of new homes are lying unfinished, building sites empty.

With the midterm elections just days away, and hugely consequential congressional races as well as the gubernatorial contest hanging in the balance, there are also political costs. Trump appears to be digging a hole for himself with Texas’s Hispanic voters.

Latino Texans who were born in the US or have naturalised, and thus can vote, are increasingly angry and confused. Many of them voted for Trump two years ago, attracted by his promise of a stronger economy and a fortified border that would keep out “criminal” immigrants.

They delivered Trump a historic victory, even in majority-Hispanic districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century – voters like Sergio Benavides, 44, the owner of a home-building construction company in the Texas borderlands of the Rio Grande valley.

A naturalised US citizen, he voted for Trump in 2024. He liked his campaign promises that he would lower prices and secure the border. When people warned him it would turn sour, he didn’t listen.

He’s listening now. The prices of homes, food and gas have all gone up. Workers have to be paid more because so many have been deported. One of his subcontractors and his wife have disappeared, picked up by ICE, leaving behind three US-citizen children.

“That makes me sad,” he said. “We are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and grow. This is not what I thought when I voted for Trump.”

Benavides is part of a backlash that is showing up in the polls. Latino voters are turning against the president on the very issues that drew them to him – the cost of living, and immigration enforcement.

A poll last month from Equis Research found that disapproval of Trump had risen to 63% among Texas Latinos. In the critical US Senate race, which could determine which party holds the upper chamber during Trump’s final two years in office, 58% of likely Latino voters intend to back the Democratic candidate James Talarico, while only 33% support the scandal-ridden Republican, Ken Paxton. This, in a state that last returned a Democrat to the US Senate in 1988.

Latinos make up a third of Texas’s registered voters, the second-highest number in the country. And they know it.

Construction workers among them.

Marco Antonio Osorio’s day begins at 5am. Same routine, six days a week.

A member of his crew comes to pick him up at his house in Houston. They drive around in their shared white truck gathering other crew, then head off to the site of a new apartment complex where they spend the next 10 hours laying TV and wifi fiber optic cables.

It’s their speciality. They are good at it, and in demand. If only they were left to get on with it.

Around the beginning of the year Osorio, 50, noticed a surge in ICE street activity. “There were so many more sheriff’s vehicles, state troopers, ICE on the highways weaving between cars checking plates.”

As an undocumented Mexican who came to the US in 1993, aged 17, he knew he was vulnerable. But he thought he had some cover. His US-born daughter Gabriela is serving as a marine at Camp Pendleton in California. She has helped him apply for residency, and the paperwork is being processed.

Still, he wasn’t taking chances. He changed his habits. No going out of the house unless for essentials. No nights out at the movies. He couldn’t stop working, or else how would he pay the bills? But now he wears a button-down shirt on the drive to the site rather than his fluorescent yellow vest. No point advertising himself as a construction worker with ICE on the hunt.

He told his company he didn’t want to work outside Houston any more. The freeways to Austin and San Antonio were crawling with cop cars. “The company told me there weren’t any jobs here – either go out of town, or you don’t work.”

So he took a job in Austin. On 10 June, as he was returning home after another 10-hour shift, a sheriff’s car did a U-turn on the freeway and pulled him over. The officer said it was because his truck had a faulty rear light, but Osorio asked himself how they could have known that as they were traveling in opposite directions. More likely, he thought, was that his vehicle has a clear front screen. “They could see we were Hispanic.”

Within two minutes of the traffic stop, ICE SUVs blocked him in, front and back. The speed with which they appeared, Osorio realised, meant it had to be coordinated.

He told them his daughter was a US marine. He showed the officers the receipt for his residency application. An ICE officer replied: “Oh, that doesn’t count.” They took him to a freezing cell, the notorious las hieleras, and from there to an immigration detention facility near the border. He spent 40 days in the wilderness of ICE custody, until Monty got him released for lack of due process.

As he awaits his appeal, Osorio continues to work. Those bills keep coming, his children need feeding. On drives to work sites in Houston, he thinks about his daughter serving the country whose government wants him gone. He worries about his youngest child, an autistic boy, and what will become of him. He imagines returning to Mexico, a place he hasn’t known for 33 years.

As he drives, he spots apartment blocks all over the city that he helped put up. And he’s proud. “See those – I worked there 10 years ago. Or those – we built them 15 years ago.”

He thinks to himself: “This is my home.”

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a Mexican national, had been in the US for 35 years, two longer than Osorio. A house framer, the skilled worker who puts up the wooden skeleton of new houses, he carried out his days with an identical drill. Out the door at 5am, pick up the crew, 10 hours of hard graft, then relax on the balcony of his self-built Houston home listening to tierra caliente music with Ñoño, his beloved dog whom he named after a podgy 1970s Mexican sitcom character.

When ICE began to crank up its street arrests in February, Salgado spotted an opportunity. Many workers were too scared to leave the house, and new homes were standing half finished. A fearless entrepreneur, Salgado began accepting jobs that other undocumented framers like him would not contemplate.

He took precautions. He swapped his construction vest for a suit jacket while driving to work. He removed the jumble of blueprints, invoices and receipts from the dashboard of his white van. It was like his mobile office on wheels, but it branded him as a building professional, so he cleaned it off.

As time passed, and the ICE presence grew more oppressive, his three sons grew concerned. They are all American-born US citizens, and Salgado had high aspirations for them. They weren’t going to be builders like him – they were going to be educated, fulfill their own American dream. Ronaldo Salgado, the eldest, is a history teacher; Lorenzo Salgado Jr studied at the prestigious Tufts University and is now an engineer in Washington DC; and the youngest is at college, also studying engineering.

The sons got together and prepared a plan for their dad. They gave him a phone number that he should call if ever he were stopped, and they made sure he carried a “know your rights” card in his wallet. They made him swear that he would never sign any ICE form, as they feared he would be hoodwinked into self-deporting.

Lorenzo Jr had an additional reason for being worried. On 29 October 2025, he was walking to work in DC. It was early morning, around the time his father would be getting on the road. That day he had a big presentation to make to a government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

As he was walking down Georgia Avenue in the direction of the White House, he saw two unmarked cars coming towards him. They passed him and then both turned around, stopping on either side of him in a pincer movement. His first thought was that he was about to be mugged. But then he realised they were federal agents. They asked him his name and where he was going. As soon as they heard his perfect English, saw his neatly buttoned shirt, and took on board his FAA destination, they backed off. “OK, go ahead, you’re good to go.”

Lorenzo Jr has no doubts he had been ethnically profiled. He was shaken by the experience. It freaked him out about his dad. If they could stop him, a Tufts-educated engineer on his way to advise the US government in the nation’s capital, what could they do to his father, an undocumented framer?

On 7 July, Lorenzo Jr got a call: his father had been stopped by ICE. He rushed to the airport and got on the first flight to Houston. Onboard the flight he saw a news report of an undocumented person in the city who had been shot by an ICE officer.

As the plane was still mid-air, Lorenzo Jr refreshed the article. The headline had been revised from “shot” to “shot, killed”.

I met Lorenzo Jr and Ronaldo Salgado in a coffee shop about 10 minutes from where their father had been shot through the window of his van after ICE mistook him for a Guatemalan national they were searching for. There was a memorial shrine to their father in a corner of the cafe, with his photo in the center surrounded by lit candles and rosaries, a few of his construction tools, a sombrero and the Mexican flag.

Both sons were still clearly stunned. But they were reflective.

Ronaldo talked about how his father had been hunted down by ICE “because he didn’t look a certain way. He didn’t match what an American is supposed to look like.”

How cruel that was, he mused, considering that his dad had spent his entire life pursuing core American values. Ronaldo rattled them off: “Work hard. Pay your taxes. Have a family. Educate them. Good things will come to you.”

Lorenzo Jr talked about how his father was killed by a government agent three days after the US celebrated its 250th birthday. On the Fourth of July, he himself had attended the fireworks in DC. He felt proud then to be an American. He recalled the history he had studied of Frederick Douglass, WEB Du Bois, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King and his biggest hero, Abraham Lincoln. He felt he was well on the way to achieving his own American dream.

Three days later, he suffered what he describes as “extreme patriotic whiplash”. Now he has only one purpose: to get justice for his dad.

Drive 350 miles south-west from Houston and you come to the border region of the Rio Grande valley. Life down here is a perfect fusion of Mexican and American. Tejano, they call it.

The valley is dusty and hot. Midday temperatures frequently hit 105F (40.5C), rising to 110F. The day I visited a building site in Harlingen, about 10 miles from the border, it was already exceeding 100F, with the sun beating down mercilessly.

Four framers were working under a cloudless sky, erecting the second-floor wooden structure of a duplex house. They were swaddled in loosely fitting clothes to protect them from the sun, with heavy tools slung around their waists. They looked unperturbed by the heat, but then this was a normal working day – 10 hours a day, six days a week.

The oldest of the four, the sombrero-wearing Joaquin, is the age that Salgado was when he was killed by ICE. Two months ago, Joaquin’s wife was taken away. She was hunted down on her way to work at a restaurant, and is now in detention awaiting deportation to Mexico.

“Now I’m scared they will grab me,” Joaquin said in Spanish. “We have three kids, born here, who will take care of them?”

His crewmate, Fortino, 38, his face hidden behind large ski glasses, is also undocumented. Two of his uncles have disappeared. “Right now, nothing is safe,” he said. “In Mexico we were taught to put our trust in God and go to work. But every single day we are looking over our shoulders, thinking that maybe today is the day they catch us.”

The third crew member, Alexis, 33, has a green card. That doesn’t stop him feeling anxious. He drives to the site now only in ordinary civilian cars, never in white vans or trucks and never with tools visible, and he regularly changes the route.

I asked him what he thinks of the argument that Trump made to the American people: that American jobs should be for Americans, not for those unlawfully residing here. Alexis laughed.

“Sure, that’s fine,” he said, also in Spanish. “But most Americans don’t do the work. They won’t do it. This is hard work, under the blazing sun. No shade. Educated Americans, they demand an office job with air-conditioning. So it’s us Latinos who do this work.”

The fourth crew member, 20-year-old Isaias, chimed in. He is a US-born citizen. Americans, he said, were used to having it easy. “Nacen en cuna de oro” – they’re born with a silver spoon in their mouths.

The four framers filled the air with the noise of banging and hammering and sawing. To my untrained ear, it seemed a healthy cacophony: the sound of a new neighbourhood, a new community, being born.

But for Ronnie Cavazos, 49, the manager of the site, the noise is symptomatic of sickness. There isn’t enough of it. It should be decibels louder. The four framers working on the house, there should be three times as many of them. Last week the site was entirely empty, he couldn’t find any crews. All his subcontractors had ceased operating.

“We don’t have enough guys to do the work – they’ve been picked up, or are too scared to leave the house, or they’ve given up and gone back to Mexico.”

Sites that were taking six months to complete are now taking 10 months. Overheads are going up. In the summer he had to pause construction for 60 days; there were no framers to call on.

Cavazos is doing all he can to protect his workers, and encourage them back on site. He has erected a fence right around the 16 duplexes he is building to keep ICE out. He expects it’ll cost him $30,000 in fencing alone, but it will be worth it if it buys some peace of mind.

He led me inside an unfinished duplex and showed me a Murphy door under the stairs. It leads to a space where workers can hide should ICE turn up.

One day his construction manager called Cavazos and alerted him to an ICE agent trying to enter the site. “I told him, ‘Get the fuck off my property!’ A lot of my workers ran away. Some went and hid behind the Murphy door.”

A few months ago he had a crew sleep on site. They were so afraid of being pulled over as they drove to work, they decided to sleep right there on the concrete foundations until the job was done.

“This is America,” Cavazos said, shaking his head. “What the fuck! This is America.”

Cavazos is chair of the South Texas Builders Association (STBA), the largest such alliance in the Rio Grande valley. He and his fellow construction leaders have decided enough is enough.

“It’s time to speak up,” Cavazos said. “A lot of people have been too afraid of what Trump will do to say anything. To stay quiet is not American. If we can’t tell the truth, what the fuck are we doing?”

In July, STBA, with the American Business Immigration Coalition Action that advocates for comprehensive immigration reform, staged what they called a “rally in the valley”. The gathering, close to the border in Pharr, Texas, concluded with a warning for Trump and the Republicans: if you carry on hunting our people, you will feel our wrath.

Benny Melendez, the owner of a small construction company in Weslaco, Texas, handles government relations for STBA. He voted for Trump in 2024, but since then 10 of his workers have been taken by ICE. As a result, his home-building projects are going up at half speed, and completed homes are costing $30,000 or more above the usual price.

As part of his lobbying duties for STBA, Melendez began gathering smartphone footage of ICE raids and posting them on social media. They show masked police and ICE agents swarming over building sites, without a warrant, apprehending workers. In one video, a framer can be seen running off the site with agents in hot pursuit, like a fox and hounds.

In another a police officer escorts several workers, hands cuffed behind their backs, from a site. “We’ll be back for the guys on the roof,” the officer threatens, adding: “It’s hot up there.”

“We’re used to it, it’s what we do,” one of the workers replies. “We probably built your house.”

Melendez made his own video to add to the collection, in which he vents his fury as a one-time Trump voter. At the start of the video we see Melendez fully masked, dressed in a black tactical utility uniform. He pulls off the mask and throws it to the ground. “Only cowards hide under a mask,” he exclaims. Next he discards his heavy armor flak jacket and replaces it with an orange construction vest and hard hat. “These are the tools we need to make America great again.”

Melendez told the Guardian that for him, the Trump administration’s assault on the Rio Grande valley amounted to a humanitarian crisis. “The dignity of our community is being walked all over.”

STBA executives decided earlier this year to blast that same message directly at the Trump administration. A delegation of seven STBA leaders, including Melendez and Cavazos and the association’s CEO, Mario Guerrero, demanded a face-to-face meeting with the Department of Homeland Security in Washington.

I wanted to hear about that meeting, so I visited Guerrero at the hub of his construction company in Edinburg, Texas. There was no mistaking his loyalties: the stars and stripes and flag of Texas dominated his office.

Guerrero describes himself as a fourth-generation Mexican-American, and a proud patriot, who voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “I’m probably more American than JD Vance. More American than Marco Rubio. Definitely more American than that damn Stephen Miller,” he said.

He voted for Trump because he was incensed by the record number of undocumented immigrants who crossed the border under Joe Biden, and because he thought Trump, as a businessman, would strengthen the valley’s economy.

But he has been dismayed since Trump’s return by the soaring prices, and by the number of hardworking, law-abiding immigrants that the administration has detained.

Guerrero told me what happened when he joined the STBA delegation to DC. They were given just 15 minutes to address top DHS officials, who sat impassively along one side of a long mahogany table.

ICE was spreading fear throughout the valley, the Texans, lined up on the other side, began. Agents were storming on to building sites without warrants, arresting people with work permits, using unmarked SUVs to hunt concrete trucks, then carting off all the workers as they poured foundations.

Shortly before the allotted time was up, the Texans were invited to give closing words. Guerrero took this as his cue. He locked eyes with the top ICE official right across the table from him. He informed him that he had voted for Trump every time he was on the ballot.

“We’re not getting what we voted for, man,” he said.

“You know what you guys are doing is fucked up. If you carry on like this, your administration is going to lose.”

articles.title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
articles.text:
Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry.

Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed.

The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year.

Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market".

"We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday.

Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland.

As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar.

Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future."

A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government".

"However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added.

Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York.

In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn.

However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games.

Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%.

General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year.

Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering".

During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed.

Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets.

Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m.

The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact.

articles.title: James Anderson not offered new contract by Lancashire
articles.text:
James Anderson's legendary career could be over after Lancashire opted against offering England's all-time leading wicket-taker a new contract.

Anderson, 44, chose to continue playing with Lancashire after England forced him into international retirement in 2024.

He captained Lancashire in the County Championship last season but the Red Rose endured a poor campaign, finishing next to bottom of Division Two.

Now, as first reported by the Times, Anderson will not be given the opportunity to play at Old Trafford in 2027 - the summer when he will turn 45.

It is not known whether Anderson will retire or look to extend his 26-year professional career with another county.

Anderson first played top-level cricket as a 17-year-old for Lancashire Cricket Board in 2000, then made his Lancashire debut the following year.

His exit from the Red Rose comes at a time of upheaval at Old Trafford. The county are undergoing a review of their cricket operations, led by interim chair Dame Sarah Storey and new chief executive Richard Kenyon. Paul Farbrace was appointed as Lancashire's director of cricket earlier this month.

Although Anderson is in his mid-40s, he has remained in supreme form in a struggling team.

He took 50 wickets in the County Championship in 2026, a tally bettered by only six other bowlers in Division Two. Anderson was named Lancashire's Championship player of the year.

Overall, 443 of Anderson's 1,193 first-class wickets came for Lancashire, to go with 83 List A wickets and 50 T20 wickets for the county.

In a 23-year international career, Anderson took 991 wickets across formats for England. Only spinners Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka and Australia's Shane Warne have more in international cricket.

In 2024, Anderson became the third bowler in Test history, after Muralitharan and Warne, to reach 700 wickets. He remains third on the all-time list with 704, a record for a pace bowler that is unlikely to be broken.

Later that year, Anderson was asked to call time on his international career by England's then hierarchy of coach Brendon McCullum, captain Ben Stokes and director of cricket Rob Key.

He played his 188th and final Test against West Indies at Lord's before embarking on a short spell as England's bowling consultant.

In 2025, Anderson signed a new deal with Lancashire and suggested he could play county cricket for three more seasons. In April of that year, he was knighted for services to cricket.

Anderson stood in as Lancashire captain during the 2025 season and was given the job full-time for 2026.

He was understood to be enjoying the role and, at the end of the this summer, there was no suggestion Anderson would end his career.

On Wednesday, as reports of his exit from Old Trafford began to emerge, those close to Anderson were unaware of the situation. Lancashire have not commented.

articles.title: Hyron Andrews: Former Sale second row died of natural causes - autopsy
articles.text:
Hyron Andrews - the former Sale second row found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match in France on Saturday - died of natural causes, an autopsy has found.

The 31-year-old, who joined the Johannesburg-based Lions this summer, suffered a tear in the aorta, an artery which carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

The rupture led to blood filling the muscle sac surrounding his heart.

Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle, with investigators working on the theory that he had either suffered a fall, a heart attack or, as transpired, an aneurysm, where a bulging blood vessel breaks.

A tear in the aorta is a rare and dangerous medical condition, which can be caused by undetected high blood pressure or a birth defect.

His body is yet to be returned to his native South Africa.

Andrews' wife Maighlin, with whom he had two young sons, has asked for "respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins", according to a statement from the Lions., external

His team-mates went ahead with their game against La Rochelle on Saturday in his honour.

The visitors were applauded into the Stade Marcel-Deflandre by home fans,, external while several of the Lions players were in tears during a minute's silence before kick-off.

Sale, with whom Andrews spent two and half seasons, also paid tribute, with director of rugby Alex Sanderson saying that his team "to a man, loved playing with Hyron and being around him".

articles.title: Formula 1: Races to return to standard distance in 2028
articles.text:
Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season.

The maximum distance of a race was cut by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season.

That reduction was introduced because of a quirk of the situation surrounding changes to the engine rules for next year.

The new hybrid engines introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have been criticised for reducing the impact of driver skill.

The power split will be changed, in two steps, to 60-40 by 2028, enabling drivers to have maximum power for longer.

This means the cars will use more fuel - and that became a concern when it emerged some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money.

As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks.

The change affects only a handful of races where fuel consumption is heaviest.

The sport's governing body, the FIA, published the 2027 rules this week and these included a section on changes for 2028 in which there is a clause that removes the reduction and reinstates the 305km maximum distance.

Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton had previously objected to the shortening of race distances.

Britain's Hamilton, 41, said: "The races should be longer because the races are physically easier than ever before. So shortening, I don't think, makes much sense.

"This is supposed to be the sport that's the most physically demanding - mentally and physically. There are some that are just so hot and ultimately you are on the edge. Like Singapore is incredibly hot and demanding.

"But that's where I think you want to see athletes - just right on the edge, right? Right at the edge of their performance, having to actually push their bodies further because that's what this sport is about - pushing, pushing the levels and pushing the boundaries."

articles.title: Why Manchester City fans boo the Premier League and Champions League anthems
articles.text:
The cacophony of boos that greet the Premier League and Champions League anthems before kick-off have now become a fixture at Etihad Stadium.

The jeers from Manchester City fans were turned up a notch against Ipswich last Saturday when the side played their first home game since being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

"I can't remember a Premier League or Champions League home game where the anthems haven't been booed," City season-ticket holder Dave Wilson told BBC Sport.

The pre-match dissatisfaction towards top-flight chiefs can likely be traced back to February 2023, when the 115 charges for breaching the rules were first announced.

Later that same year, Everton had 10 points - reduced to six on appeal - deducted after being found to have broken profit and sustainability rules.

In their first game back after the sanction, Toffees fans displayed their ire at Goodison Park by loudly booing the league's pre-match anthem as well as holding up red cards with the word 'corrupt' printed underneath the Premier League logo.

Though City supporters did not organise a similar display, their anger was clear.

"The Premier League anthem has been booed by City fans for many years," said Wilson. "It was probably heightened on Saturday because it was the first home game since the [guilty verdict] announcement.

"There hasn't been much love lost between City and the Premier League for a long time. For certain games it will be louder than others, it definitely wasn't co-ordinated for that [Ipswich] game but a symptom of everything coming together."

There was audible booing before Tuesday's Champions League fixture against AEK Athens too.

City fans' displeasure towards Uefa goes back even further, there being a litany of disputes with Europe's top brass.

In 2012, Porto were handed a fine, external of around £17,000 by Uefa after City made a complaint of racial abuse towards striker Mario Balotelli to the organising body.

In that same season, City were given a fine, external of around £24,000 for being one minute late back on to the pitch for the second half of a game against Sporting.

In 2014, Uefa fined City £49m and capped their squad size for the Champions League after they failed Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules.

Six years later, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned City's two-year ban from European club competitions after clearing them of "disguising equity funds as sponsorship contributions" - Uefa initially ruled City had committed "serious breaches" of FFP regulations between 2012 and 2016.

Wilson adds: "City fans generally feel there is a conspiracy against them, like the booing of the Uefa anthem too. There is a feeling of being targeted, rightly or wrongly.

"City fans just don't seem to like the competitions we play in!"

City and their supporters are currently in limbo as they await the outcome of the appeal and any potential sanctions.

The side are currently top of the table having won all seven league games so far and that 100% record will be given a stern examination with a difficult trip to Aston Villa on Saturday (kick-off 12:30 BST).

Nick Clarke is interim chair of The Citizens Trust - Manchester City supporters' union, a member-led trust that was set up earlier this year at a time when the "potential biggest issue affecting City fans in the club's history" had transpired.

Though it has been a "difficult time", fans are "completely behind the team" and he says his job is to ensure their views are heard amid the external noise.

"The booing of the anthem on Saturday was totally organic," says Clarke. "Whereas the bananas at Liverpool was a fan-led initiative co-ordinated by the 1894 atmosphere group and they did great work handing those out before the game.

"Even though there are fans who are conflicted about what has happened with the club, there is still a general feeling among the majority [of City fans] that the Premier League is not fit for purpose in regulating itself and how it is ran."

Whatever the outcome of the appeal, City fans are likely to continue making their feelings clear before kick-off.

articles.title: Canada v England: Ellie Kildunne on bench as Red Roses ring changes
articles.text:
England head coach John Mitchell says Ellie Kildunne needs to show greater consistency after dropping his star full-back to the bench in the wake of the Red Roses' first defeat in four years.

Kildunne was part of the starting XV that lost 24-21 to Canada last Friday in Toronto as England's unbeaten streak ended at 41 matches.

"It is undisputed that she adds huge value," said Mitchell of the 27-year-old.

"She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to to help her through that.

"She wants to become consistent as well and she'll get back.

"It's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game and that goes for everyone."

Emma Sing comes in at full-back in Kildunne's place for Saturday's rematch (00:10 BST) against Canada in Ottawa, while Tatyana Heard and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald - backline starters in the defeat - drop out of the matchday squad entirely.

Helena Rowland and Mia Venner replace Heard and Moloney-MacDonald at inside centre and wing respectively.

In the fourth change to the starting line-up, Sadia Kabeya, who appeared off the bench last week on her comeback from a leg injury, starts with Alex Matthews, two-time Rugby World Cup winner, dropping to the bench.

Exeter's Flo Robinson and Sale's Hollie Aitchison are included on the bench as a new-look set of half-back replacements.

Sing, a rangy runner who can also kick goals, started two matches at full-back during England's Six Nations campaign, with Kildunne switching to a different position on the wing on each occasion.

Sing's Gloucester-Hartpury team-mate Venner made her England debut in 2020 aged just 17.

Venner has won only another four caps since but was putting pressure on England's more established back three at the start of this year, appearing in wins over Scotland and Italy.

The 24-year-old finished as the PWR's joint top try-scorer last season, crossing 12 times.

Moloney-MacDonald cost her side an early try in the defeat by Canada when, after doing superbly to pick Jess Breach's pass off her toes, she spilled the ball over the line in the sixth minute.

"Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most. That's on us to fix," added Mitchell.

"This week is about getting back to who we are - hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could."We've earned a strong period but nothing about it is owed to us going forward.

"Friday [Saturday 00:10 BST] is an opportunity to apply sustained pressure, learn from what we missed and come out the other side better than we went in."

articles.title: Mark Allen: Former world number one says he spent time in mental health clinic before snooker return
articles.text:
Mark Allen says he is working to "turn things around" and revealed he spent time in a mental health clinic before returning to snooker.

The former world number one lost to friend Jordan Brown in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open on Tuesday after five months away from the sport.

Speaking after the match, an emotional Allen said he was in a "bad place at the minute" and considering retirement.

"Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I'm doing my best to turn things round," Northern Ireland's Allen said in a statement on X on Wednesday.

He said he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself so he could prepare for Tuesday's match against Brown, adding that he plans to continue his treatment.

"I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter, to see me play for what could be the last time. I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour," added the 40-year-old.

"I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular Simon Brownell [CEO] and Neil Tomkins [World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association COO] who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself."

The World Snooker Tour (WST) said they and the WPBSA are "supporting Mark and wish to help in any way we can".

articles.title: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia injury: PSG forward to have surgery on ruptured ACL
articles.text:
Paris St-Germain winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia will undergo knee surgery after rupturing his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) during his side's 4-2 win over Barcelona on Tuesday.

Kvaratskhelia sustained the injury during a challenge with Xavi Espart and was unable to put weight on his right leg as he was substituted in the 59th minute of the Champions League tie.

PSG have not put a timeline on his return to action.

In a statement on Instagram, Kvaratskhelia said: "Before every game I play I ask God to leave the field healthy, but in vain.

"I probably prepared for this game the best I have ever prepared for. I thought I was prepared for everything.

"I realise that God chose me and if I protected the players on another field, I'm ready to go through these months of hard work, pain, tears.

"I know I have to come back stronger for my people who always have my back. I won't let you down, I promise, I won't waste a second."

Kvaratskhelia, 25, helped PSG win back-to-back Champions League titles following his move to the French capital from Napoli in January 2025.

The Georgia international has featured 11 times for PSG this season.

The club also confirmed Ousmane Dembele and Marquinhos will be absent for a "few weeks". Dembele limped off with a left thigh injury while Marquinhos injured his right thigh.

PSG and Barcelona were level at 2-2 heading into the final 10 minute at Parc des Princes before the hosts scored twice late on to maintain their winning start to their Champions League defence. They sit top of the table with three wins from three matches.

articles.title: Lord's digs up cricket pitch - why the drastic action and what next?
articles.text:
It is the sight no-one has seen for a generation.

Diggers in front of Lord's famous old pavilion. A gaping hole in the middle of the square.

After years of issues and complaints around the playing surface at cricket's spiritual home, those in charge have taken the drastic step to dig up one of its strips.

So what caused it, what is being done and what does it mean for the future?

The strip in question is Pitch Nine.

Lord's has 20 across the square but nine is one of five central strips used for the most high-profile matches.

Crucially, it was the controversial surface used for England's Test against New Zealand in June - a surface that proved incredibly difficult for batting.

Jacob Bethell was bowled by a ball that shot along the ground and the Test would have been over inside two days had it not been for bad weather.

Afterwards, England captain Ben Stokes said the surface does not benefit Test cricket and it was rated as "unsatisfactory" by the International Cricket Council.

Cricket's most historic venue had to deal with the ignominy of a demerit point being placed on its record.

The New Zealand Test was not the first case of Lord's - which is effectively guaranteed at least two Tests per year by the England and Wales Cricket Board - having trouble with its playing surface.

The pitches used for the men's Tests against Ireland in 2019, New Zealand in 2021 and Australia in 2023, plus a women's one-day international against India in 2022, were all rated "average" under the ICC's previous system.

Lord's has often been criticised for being slow and low, thus providing less entertaining cricket.

Back in February, the MCC stated the "square must be at the forefront of the club's priorities" and in the summer it set out a seven-point "pitch action plan", which has included bringing in external experts.

As reported by Cricinfo, external, this month things have gone a step further.

Over five days, Pitch Nine was dug up and the 22-yard hole filled with a base layer of gravel.

The area has been rolled and tended to by the groundstaff and fresh soil was added on top. It now looks little different to the square around it.

But this is not the end of the story.

In a letter sent to members last week, the MCC chair Mark Nicholas warned "we should all be braced for the scheduling challenges" their pitch plans will bring.

Pitch Nine will be out of action until 2029 at the earliest, depriving Lord's of one of its main TV pitches.

Major matches next year include the second men's Ashes Test in late June, a women's Ashes one-day international in July, a men's Test against Bangladesh in May, and a men's ODI in September.

Lord's plans to cope as best it can and the MCC has also stepped up its plans around hybrid pitches.

Lord's already has two hybrids, where synthetic fibres are inserted and mixed with a regular grass pitch, and a third will be added to the square in the spring.

Hybrids are not currently allowed in Test cricket but are allowed in white-ball internationals and domestic cricket.

They can be revitalised and reused more quickly than natural surfaces, which could relieve some of the pressure caused by the loss of Pitch Nine.

And Lord's is also continuing with its plans to introduce drop-in surfaces.

Drop-ins - pitches which are grown away from the main square before being 'dropped' into place - are common in Australia and New Zealand but not in the UK.

After Nicholas said earlier this year drop-ins could be used as early as 2028, the first trays will be introduced to the Nursery Ground in the coming weeks.

"The work now underway represents the most comprehensive review of the square and pitch preparation at Lord's in a generation," Nicholas told members.

"While these changes will take time to deliver their full benefit, they will help to ensure that the club prepares pitches worthy of the ground's reputation."

Time will tell whether the changes are as successful as hoped.

articles.title: Beth Dobbin writes to Andy Burnham calling for increased funding into ME research
articles.text:
Former British sprinter Beth Dobbin has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to fund more research into the "life-decimating" condition that has resulted in her spending 22 hours a day in bed.

On Friday, 32-year-old Dobbin - who raced at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago - revealed in an interview with BBC Sport she had been diagnosed with ME (myalgic encephalomyelitis).

ME is a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.

It has no known cure or specific treatment. More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.

In a letter to Burnham, external, Dobbin said: "ME has been neglected and psychologicalised for years.

"It has received so little government funding for research over the years compared to other illnesses. As a consequence, there are no approved treatments.

"There are also currently no provisions within the NHS for severe ME patients (25% of those with ME). What other illness this prevalent would leave patients with nowhere to go within the NHS, or no specialists other than to seek private care?"

ME patients often rely on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.

A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.

Dobbin, who has left the house on just five occasions this year, decided to do the interview with BBC Sport in a bid to raise awareness of the condition, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

"Your government has said it wants to bring down the welfare bill," Dobbin continued in her letter to Burnham.

She added: "ME is so debilitating, severe patients are violently unwell, bedbound and can't even look after themselves, let alone work.

"To get the welfare bill down, I believe you need to fund research into this spiralling illness and help us all get our lives back."

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has vowed to reduce the UK's welfare bill.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030-31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Between April 2019 and March 2024 the UK government invested around £6.5 million in research into ME.

Earlier this year, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, it announced an investment of £4.75 million into a world-first genomics study into the condition.

BBC Sport has contacted No 10 for comment.

articles.title: Animal rights group Peta asks Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot
articles.text:
An animal rights group is urging Crystal Palace to retire their live bald eagle mascot with immediate effect, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals".

In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) asked the Premier League club to stop using the eagle, named Phoenix, in pre-match displays at Selhurst Park and to never use live animal mascots again.

The London team, known as the Eagles since 1973, introduced a live eagle to matchdays in 2010. Kayla, who died in 2020, performed the role for 10 years and her replacement Phoenix made her debut against West Ham in August 2024.

Peta says birds can become "frightened, disoriented and panicked" in stadium environments, putting themselves and fans at risk.

Using them for displays and entertainment also denies the animals, who "would naturally avoid humans", the opportunity to engage with their natural instincts, leading to "frustration and stress", the group said.

The organisation has "detailed records" of incidents involving live mascots, including birds, being injured or killed in collisions with walls, windows and match balls, as well as a falcon embedding its talons in a spectator's scalp after landing on his head.

In 2017, a Charlton Athletic fan was found guilty of trying to punch Kayla the eagle at a League Cup fixture two years earlier.

"Many professional sports teams use only willing humans as mascots and the club already has Pete the Eagle to excite the crowd," said Dr Carys Bennett, Peta's senior corporate projects manager.

"Bald eagles are widely recognised as symbols of freedom. They deserve better than to be used as an entertainment prop to amuse the Eagles' fans."

articles.title: Eberechi Eze: Why is he struggling at Arsenal?
articles.text:
This is not the first time Eze's role in the squad has been called into question.

He switched off when Matty Cash scored Aston Villa's opener in their 2-1 defeat in December 2025 and, despite starting the following game, was left on the substitute's bench for the next four league matches.

And while the 28-year-old is a much-loved character around both the Arsenal and England squads, even Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel referenced how Eze was "coming back to his true shape and form" in training during the last international break - hinting that he has not been at his best so far this season.

The reason Eze's performance is coming under scrutiny now is that the Gunners failed to land a new world-class attacker in the transfer window, despite being heavily interested in Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr and Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez.

Arsenal signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge in the summer and the Greek international had been the first-choice winger for Mikel Arteta this season, until he picked up a hamstring injury on international duty.

Tzolis being out of action presented an opportunity for Eze to break into the squad again, scoring in a start on the left wing against Lille in the Champions League - but he was unable to follow that up against Forest.

"I think that finding his role and position has been challenging," former Arsenal and England defender Matt Upson said.

"And when you come to a club with the stature and the quality of Arsenal, if you're not showing that you're nailing down a certain role, I think it's very very hard to maintain a position in the team.

"He's now filling in a bit on the left-hand side, which I don't think particularly suits him, but he's had to.

"He doesn't play like a wide player for me and I think just knowing your role when you're at a club like Arsenal is so important."

Eze scored some spectacular goals in big moments when he was at Crystal Palace, including the winner in the FA Cup final against Manchester City in 2025.

"I think all the high-end stuff that we saw from him which made him a player that Arsenal were going to go and target, that's the icing on the cake," said Upson.

"So when the foundation's not quite there in terms of the situations you're getting in and how quickly you get into the ball, where you are on the field, where your headspace is at about what your role is and what you've got to do, then it's hard to produce those moments that make you the top player."

Eze shone from the left at Palace, but in his final two seasons in south London he operated from a narrower number 10 role.

But with captain Martin Odegaard the first choice in that position at Arsenal and Arteta unlikely to start the pair regularly with the options he has available in the middle of the pitch, it means Eze's route into the team is limited.

Upson believes Eze must understand what is wanted from him.

"It's almost a process for him if he wants to kind of grow into starting more matches for Arsenal," he said.

"I think figuring that out is really important and having that level of intensity, which I think has been an adjustment for him from where he's come from - into a big club, with a manager that they don't come more intense than really."

articles.title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
articles.text:
Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.

The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts.

Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.

"Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity.

In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."

"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."

Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority, saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force".

But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight.

After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said.

Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, external, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.

The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for.

Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns.

Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future."

"Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.

In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities.

The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data.

Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up.

Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation."

However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year.

Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year, allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control".

Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.

As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.

"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.

"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."

Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.

"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".

Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."

Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]."

"Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.

Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".

Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.

Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi

articles.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued
articles.text:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.

The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.

"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.

Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.

And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.

Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.

They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.

Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance, external" without specifying the reason.

The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws.

OpenAI said in a blog post, external it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade.

"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.

It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.

The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.

Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.

"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.

Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external.

"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.

Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.

The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.

"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.

He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".

The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".

Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.

Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".

The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".

It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.

The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.

PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.

Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
articles.text:
Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the suspect's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who police say then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

DNA science isn't the only technology that is helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major investigations like the hunt for Sperino's attacker is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating her murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?
articles.text:
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.

Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.

Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.

Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.

Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.

The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.

Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle".

Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.

Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.

He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.

But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.

"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.

SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%.

Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.

In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.

Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.

Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.

However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.

Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.

"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.

The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
articles.text:
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.

A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.

Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.

The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.

District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".

"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.

The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.

In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.

However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.

The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.

The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".

Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.
